paragraphs: Combining several models can improve predictions, but an ensemble also needs to describe how uncertain those predictions are. This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric ensemble approach, called BNE, that augments an existing ensemble to account for different sources of uncertainty. Its purpose includes both estimating uncertainty accurately and explaining its origins.

BNE modifies the model’s prediction and distribution functions using Bayesian nonparametric methods. This gives the augmentation a role in representing uncertainty patterns across the data distribution. The paper provides a theoretical guarantee for robustly estimating those patterns and shows how overall predictive uncertainty can be separated into components associated with different sources of noise and error.

The reported results show accurate uncertainty estimates in the presence of complex observational noise. An application to air pollution exposure prediction in Eastern Massachusetts illustrates how the decomposition can help detect model bias. The practical contribution is therefore richer than an uncertainty value attached to a prediction: it also offers information about what contributes to that uncertainty.
neurips-2019-accurate-uncertainty-estima.tldr: BNE augments ensembles to estimate predictive uncertainty and separate contributions from different sources of noise and error.

paragraphs: When organizations run many experiments in sequence, they need to limit false discoveries while still detecting real effects. Online false discovery rate control addresses this as tests arrive. The paper focuses on a practical obstacle: existing adaptive methods can lose considerable detection power when p-values under true null hypotheses tend to be larger than uniformly distributed values.

The proposed algorithm, ADDIS, uses adaptive discarding and comes with a proof of false discovery rate control. Its central aim is to exploit the conservative behavior of null p-values so that valid error control does not come with such a large loss of useful discoveries. This targets a distributional feature that the abstract describes as common in practice.

The authors report appreciable power improvements over existing methods when null p-values are conservative. When they are exactly uniform, ADDIS rarely loses power; this is a qualified claim, not a promise of improvement in every setting. The work also offers guidance on robust tuning choices and extends the discarding idea to asynchronous experiments and offline testing.
neurips-2019-addis-an-adaptive-discardin.tldr: ADDIS controls online false discoveries while improving detection power when null p-values are conservative.

paragraphs: Disease progression models can predict patient risk, but those predictions do not necessarily provide an understandable account of how a disease develops. This paper introduces an attentive state-space model intended to support both goals. It learns structured representations of disease trajectories while using those representations to predict future patient outcomes.

The key modeling choice is to let future disease states depend on past medical history through attention weights. In the Markovian models discussed in the abstract, the dynamics are memoryless. Here, attention explicitly represents dependence on earlier history, giving the model a way to express which parts of that history matter for future disease states.

The authors also develop an inference procedure that learns model parameters together with an inference network. It uses the attentive structure to construct a Rao-Blackwellized variational approximation to the distribution of disease states. Experiments with the UK Cystic Fibrosis registry report superior predictive accuracy and insights into chronic disease progression, supporting the model’s combined emphasis on prediction and interpretable trajectories.
neurips-2019-attentive-state-space-model.tldr: An attentive state-space model uses medical history to learn interpretable disease trajectories and improve outcome prediction.

paragraphs: A probabilistic classifier should express uncertainty accurately, especially when its predictions inform consequential decisions. In classification with several possible classes, checking only the probability assigned to the most confident choice can leave important aspects of calibration unexamined. This paper develops a broader framework for measuring calibration across multiclass predictions.

The proposed measures generalize several existing approaches, including expected calibration error, maximum calibration error, and maximum mean calibration error. For a particular family built using matrix-valued kernels, the authors propose and empirically evaluate consistent and unbiased estimators. The framework therefore connects familiar calibration summaries with a more general mathematical treatment.

A central contribution is interpreting these estimators as statistical test quantities under the hypothesis that the model is calibrated. The authors provide bounds and approximations for the associated p-values. This gives calibration measurements a clearer statistical meaning than an isolated score with no natural scale, helping readers assess evidence of miscalibration rather than relying solely on the numerical size of an error measure.
neurips-2019-calibration-tests-in-multi-.tldr: A unified framework turns multiclass calibration measures into statistically interpretable tests of predictive uncertainty.

paragraphs: Generating an image from text becomes more useful when changing a description can selectively change the relevant visual content. This paper introduces ControlGAN, a generative adversarial network designed to produce high-quality images and manipulate particular parts through natural language. Its goal is to connect individual textual changes with specific visual attributes.

The generator uses attention at the word level across spatial locations and channels. This helps separate visual attributes and focus generation on regions associated with relevant words. A word-level discriminator supplies detailed feedback by relating words to image regions, supporting the generator’s ability to change selected attributes while preserving other content.

The method also uses perceptual loss to reduce randomness in generation and encourage changes corresponding to the modified text. Experiments on benchmark datasets report performance beyond existing state-of-the-art approaches and demonstrate effective manipulation of synthetic images through descriptions. Together, these components address the connection between text and image at a finer level than treating the whole description as one undifferentiated instruction.
neurips-2019-controllable-text-to-image-.tldr: ControlGAN links words to visual regions and attributes so text changes can selectively modify generated images.

paragraphs: Decision-making environments often contain related states and coordinated sequences of actions. Two states may describe similar physical configurations, making their transition behavior related as well. This paper asks how a learning system for discrete environments can explicitly represent such correlations, instead of treating related parts of the problem as unrelated.

The authors introduce a Bayesian learning framework based on Pólya-Gamma augmentation. It is designed to incorporate correlation structure into reasoning about discrete decision problems. This matters because the structure of an environment can provide information beyond isolated observations: relationships among states or actions can help the model learn from the data it receives.

The framework is demonstrated on imitation learning, subgoal extraction, system identification, and Bayesian reinforcement learning. Across the reported applications, explicitly modeling correlations yields better predictive performance than models that ignore them, even with training datasets an order of magnitude smaller. These findings support the value of representing the relevant correlations in the studied problems, particularly when available observations are limited.
neurips-2019-correlation-priors-for-rein.tldr: A Bayesian framework models correlations in discrete decision problems to improve predictions with substantially less training data.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders with discrete hidden variables face a training difficulty: choosing among discrete alternatives introduces an operation that ordinary differentiation cannot directly handle. The Gumbel-Max trick provides a way to reparameterize these variables, but its final argmax operation selects a single alternative and leaves the resulting objective nondifferentiable.

The paper proposes applying direct loss minimization to optimize this objective. Previous approaches discussed in the abstract replace the hard selection with a softmax-based relaxation. The proposed method instead addresses the objective containing the discrete choice directly, offering another route for training models whose hidden representations involve categorical decisions.

The approach also extends to structured discrete latent variables, where choices have relationships rather than being independent alternatives. This extension depends on being able to compute the required argmax tractably. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of direct loss minimization for both unstructured and structured discrete variational autoencoders, supporting its use across these two kinds of latent-variable models.
neurips-2019-direct-optimization-through.tldr: Direct loss minimization trains discrete variational autoencoders through hard argmax choices without using softmax relaxations.

paragraphs: Compressive learning reduces the burden of high-dimensional data by randomly projecting it into a smaller space before learning. This paper studies an additional compression step: scalar quantization of the projected values. The resulting question is how this extra loss of numerical detail affects a model’s ability to generalize beyond its training examples.

The authors derive generalization error bounds for nearest-neighbor classification, linear classification, and least-squares regression. Their analysis covers finite training samples as well as asymptotic behavior. In the asymptotic analysis, they connect classification performance to the variance of debiased inner-product estimators, linking the quality of an underlying numerical estimate to the learning task.

By isolating the additional error introduced by quantization, the work provides guidance for selecting quantizers for different applications. The value of a compression choice is therefore considered in relation to what the learner must do with the compressed data. An empirical study validates the theoretical findings, connecting the error analysis with observed behavior.
neurips-2019-generalization-error-analys.tldr: The paper bounds how quantizing randomly projected data affects generalization in classification and regression.

paragraphs: Regression with heavy-tailed or contaminated data often benefits from robust losses. The problem becomes harder when predictions contain multiple labels whose relationships must also be represented. This paper studies robust alternatives for these structured settings, where a Gaussian Markov random field likelihood is often used despite the challenges posed by unusual or corrupted observations.

The analysis focuses on losses derived from elliptical distributions, a family that includes many previously proposed losses. These objectives are nonconvex, so ordinary optimization could potentially stop at a stationary point that is worse than another solution. The paper investigates whether the algebraic structure of these particular problems changes that concern.

Its central theoretical result applies in the limit of infinite training data: every stationary point is globally optimal. That qualification matters because the guarantee concerns the limiting problem rather than an unrestricted claim about finite datasets. The authors also demonstrate the empirical appeal of these losses on synthetic and real data, supporting their practical interest for robust structured regression.
neurips-2019-globally-optimal-learning-f.tldr: For structured elliptical losses, the paper proves global optimality of all stationary points in the infinite-data limit.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires deciding which earlier actions deserve credit for an eventual outcome. This paper proposes using the outcome itself as new information when making that judgment. The guiding question is how likely a past decision was to have led to what was subsequently observed, giving the learner an explicit hindsight-based perspective.

This changes how information from an experience is used. Rather than assigning credit only through expectations formed before the outcome, the method looks back after the outcome is known. The authors show that value functions can be rewritten in terms of this perspective, connecting the idea to a central object already used in reinforcement learning.

That reformulation produces a family of algorithms whose properties the authors study. Experiments on illustrative tasks show that these algorithms address important credit-assignment challenges. The reported evidence supports hindsight as a useful way to extract learning signals from observed outcomes, while the value-function reformulation explains how the idea can become a concrete learning procedure.
neurips-2019-hindsight-credit-assignment.tldr: Hindsight credit assignment uses observed outcomes to reassess which past decisions should receive credit.

paragraphs: A classifier can struggle when an input undergoes a spatial transformation, even though its relevant identity remains the same. This paper studies regularizers that encourage predictions to stay invariant under such transformations. It provides theoretical and empirical evidence that these training incentives can improve accuracy on examples transformed in the worst case.

On CIFAR-10, standard and adversarial training with the proposed regularization achieve a 20% relative error reduction on adversarially transformed examples under the same computational budget. The reported results also exceed those of handcrafted spatial-equivariant networks. This supports regularization as an effective way to encourage spatial robustness within the evaluated training settings.

The authors additionally observe improved ordinary test accuracy from robust training on SVHN, a dataset with inherent orientation variation. They prove a corresponding absence of an accuracy–robustness trade-off for adversarial examples arising from transformation groups. The scope of that result matters: it concerns this structured class of transformations and explains why robustness and standard accuracy can improve together in the setting studied.
neurips-2019-invariance-inducing-regular.tldr: Regularization that encourages spatial invariance improves robustness, with evidence that suitable transformation settings can also improve standard accuracy.

paragraphs: Large recommendation systems must find relevant items quickly within enormous collections. A tree index helps organize that search, while a preference model estimates which parts of the tree suit a user. This paper argues that the quality of these two components is interdependent, making their joint learning important for recommendation accuracy.

The proposed framework trains the index structure and the user-preference prediction model under a shared performance measure. This aligns how the collection is organized with how the model evaluates candidate items. The authors also introduce a hierarchical representation of user preferences that makes use of the structure provided by the tree.

The approach builds on tree-based retrieval, whose existing TDM formulation enables logarithmic computational complexity relative to collection size. The paper’s reported contribution is improved recommendation accuracy through joint optimization. Evaluations on two large real-world datasets show significant gains, and an online A/B test on a display advertising platform demonstrates effectiveness in production. These findings support treating indexing and preference learning as connected design problems.
neurips-2019-joint-optimization-of-tree-.tldr: Jointly learning a recommendation tree and user-preference model improves accuracy in large-scale evaluations and a production A/B test.

paragraphs: A model that generates convincing images may also learn useful ways to represent visual information. This paper investigates that connection for adversarial generative models. Although GANs had shown early promise for unsupervised representation learning, self-supervised methods had overtaken them, motivating a fresh look as image-generation quality improved.

The authors introduce BigBiGAN by extending BigGAN with an encoder and changing the discriminator. The encoder adds a way to obtain representations from images, allowing the generative approach to serve a representation-learning purpose. This connects advances in image synthesis with the goal of learning useful visual features without supervised labels.

Extensive evaluations examine both learned representations and image generation. The reported models achieve state-of-the-art unsupervised representation learning on ImageNet while also producing compelling unconditional images. These results show that the generation improvements used in this work translate into substantially better representations. The contribution is evidence that strong generative modeling can support both image synthesis and competitive unsupervised visual learning within the evaluated setting.
neurips-2019-large-scale-adversarial-rep.tldr: BigBiGAN extends a strong image generator with an encoder to achieve leading unsupervised ImageNet representations and compelling image synthesis.

paragraphs: This paper studies an attack that modifies training examples with bounded perturbations so a trained classifier behaves incorrectly on clean test inputs. The intended manipulation can be untargeted, reducing performance generally, or targeted toward particular prediction rules. The focus is on influencing what a classifier learns through altered training data.

The method trains an autoencoder-like perturbation generator alongside an imagined differentiable victim classifier. The generator learns changes intended to steer the victim’s training trajectory toward poor test performance. The resulting optimization has nonlinear equality constraints, and the authors propose decoupling alternating updates of the two networks to make the procedure more stable.

The method can also be extended to label-specific manipulation, where predictions follow predefined attacker objectives. Experiments on several datasets, including CIFAR-10 and a reduced ImageNet dataset, support its effectiveness. The reported perturbations also transfer well across different victim classifier types. This empirical transfer is significant because the generator is learned with an imagined victim, while the intended effects extend to other tested classifiers.
neurips-2019-learning-to-confuse-generat.tldr: An autoencoder-like generator learns bounded training-data perturbations that impair clean-test predictions and transfer across tested classifiers.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning tries to make useful training data out of examples that lack labels, reducing dependence on expensive labeled datasets. MixMatch combines several dominant ideas in this area into one algorithm. Its central contribution is an integrated training procedure that brings labeled and unlabeled examples into a shared learning process.

The algorithm guesses low-entropy labels for augmented unlabeled examples, meaning its guessed label distributions are relatively concentrated. It then uses MixUp to mix labeled and unlabeled data. These steps connect the creation of training targets for unlabeled examples with the way the combined data is presented during learning.

The paper reports substantial improvements across multiple datasets and amounts of labeled data. On CIFAR-10 with 250 labels, error falls from 38% to 11%; on STL-10, the reported reduction is by a factor of two. The authors also demonstrate an improved accuracy–privacy trade-off under differential privacy and use an ablation study to examine which components contribute most to MixMatch’s success.
neurips-2019-mixmatch-a-holistic-approac.tldr: MixMatch combines guessed labels for augmented unlabeled data with MixUp to substantially improve semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Decision tree ensembles are usually represented through their branching structures. MonoForest converts each tree into a polynomial form, giving the same model a different mathematical representation. The paper uses this representation for three purposes: understanding ensemble behavior, reducing model size, and translating between tree forms that may have different practical advantages.

The polynomial form supports a straightforward interpretation of the original ensemble. Experiments report results comparable with leading interpretation techniques. It also enables pruning across the ensemble by removing polynomial terms according to training-data statistics. The authors report reducing model size by as much as a factor of three without a loss of quality in their experiments.

The framework additionally identifies equivalence between classes of tree shapes that share a polynomial representation. This makes it possible to train using one shape and use another that is easier to compute or interpret. The authors formulate optimal translation between forms as a problem and develop a greedy solution, extending the framework from analysis to model transformation.
neurips-2019-monoforest-framework-for-tr.tldr: MonoForest represents tree ensembles as polynomials to support interpretation, pruning, and translation between equivalent tree shapes.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate different factors underlying complex observations. This paper investigates whether that property helps make downstream predictions fairer. The setting involves observations, such as images, that depend on both a prediction target and a sensitive variable that is not observed during learning.

The authors show that both optimal predictions and predictions learned empirically can be unfair in this setting, even when the target and sensitive variable are independent. Independence between those variables therefore does not by itself settle the fairness of predictions made from the learned representation. This motivates examining the representation as part of the problem.

The empirical analysis covers representations from more than 12,600 trained disentanglement models. Several disentanglement scores consistently correlate with increased fairness. That finding suggests encouraging disentanglement may be useful when sensitive variables are unavailable. The evidence is an observed association between particular scores and fairness, preserving a distinction between a promising representation property and a guarantee that downstream predictions will be fair.
neurips-2019-on-the-fairness-of-disentan.tldr: Several disentanglement scores correlate with fairer downstream predictions, suggesting potential value when sensitive variables are unobserved.

paragraphs: Numerical integration can approximate an integral using a weighted collection of function evaluations. Determinantal point processes, or DPPs, choose evaluation points with repulsion between them, with that dependence controlled by a kernel. This paper examines two unbiased Monte Carlo estimators that use this sampling structure.

The authors revisit the Ermakov–Zolotukhin estimator, which computes weights by solving a linear system, and analyze it using modern methods. They also provide an efficient exact sampler for a multidimensional DPP called the multivariate Jacobi ensemble. This process meets the assumptions of the central limit theorem associated with the Bardenet–Hardy estimator, enabling further investigation of both approaches.

Experiments show favorable behavior when the kernel matches a function basis in which the integrand has few nonzero coefficients or rapidly decreasing coefficients. The choice of estimator depends on available knowledge: when the basis and sparsity level are known, the Ermakov–Zolotukhin estimator can be suitable. Otherwise, it can behave erratically, making that qualification central to interpreting its usefulness.
neurips-2019-on-two-ways-to-use-determin.tldr: The paper analyzes two DPP-based integration estimators and shows how their usefulness depends on matching kernels to integrand structure.

paragraphs: Large Transformer language models may exceed the capacity of a single computing device, requiring their computation to be divided across devices. This form of model parallelism creates training challenges. The paper identifies backward locking during backpropagation, along with the inapplicability of some existing methods to language models, as obstacles to efficient training.

Ouroboros introduces a model-parallel algorithm designed to accelerate Transformer-based language-model training. Its contribution addresses how training proceeds across the divided model. The authors also provide a convergence guarantee to critical points for nonconvex problems, connecting the proposed training procedure with a formal optimization result.

Experiments on Transformer and Transformer-XL language models report substantial speedups beyond data parallelism, with comparable or better accuracy. This supports the practical value of distributing a model’s training computation effectively when model size makes distribution necessary. The theoretical result concerns convergence to critical points; the reported accuracy and speed evidence comes from the evaluated language-model experiments.
neurips-2019-ouroboros-on-accelerating-t.tldr: Ouroboros accelerates model-parallel Transformer training, with a critical-point convergence guarantee and comparable or better experimental accuracy.

paragraphs: Lipschitz constraints bound how much a network’s output can change as its input changes. Such bounds are useful for provable adversarial robustness, stable training, and Wasserstein distance estimation. Building networks from individually constrained layers can enforce these bounds, but gradients may progressively shrink, creating an obstacle to effective learning.

This paper extends a gradient-norm-preserving approach from fully connected networks to convolutional networks. Its main construction is Block Convolution Orthogonal Parameterization, or BCOP, an expressive way to parameterize orthogonal convolution operations. The aim is to retain useful learning behavior while enforcing a provable constraint on the network.

The authors also address the disconnected structure of the space of orthogonal convolutions. They show that the largest connected component of BCOP with twice as many channels can represent arbitrary BCOP convolutions at the original channel count. The parameterization enables large convolutional networks with provable Lipschitz bounds, and experiments find competitive performance for certified adversarial robustness and Wasserstein distance estimation.
neurips-2019-preventing-gradient-attenua.tldr: BCOP enables scalable, provably Lipschitz convolutional networks by extending gradient-preserving orthogonal constructions to convolutions.

paragraphs: Neural pathways contain abundant feedback connections as well as connections carrying information forward. This paper investigates what feedback can contribute to retrieving information organized into categories at multiple levels. The authors study a hierarchical network that stores categorical information about objects and retrieves it progressively, moving from coarse categories toward finer distinctions.

The model uses dynamic positive and negative feedback from higher layers to lower layers. These two forms of feedback serve different roles: positive feedback suppresses interference associated with correlations between different categories, while negative feedback suppresses interference associated with correlations within the same category. Their combined action improves retrieval performance significantly.

This account gives push and pull complementary functions within one retrieval process. The model agrees with a push-pull phenomenon observed in neural data, linking its proposed mechanism to an experimental observation. The contribution is a mechanistic explanation within the studied network of how feedback can reduce interference and improve hierarchical retrieval, offering insight into the broader role of feedback in neural information processing.
neurips-2019-push-pull-feedback-implemen.tldr: A hierarchical neural model shows how positive and negative feedback jointly suppress interference and improve information retrieval.

paragraphs: Posterior sampling offers an effective way to balance exploration with using what an agent already knows. Randomized value functions are a promising route to scaling that idea. This paper shows, however, that most contemporary combinations of randomized value functions and neural networks lack properties responsible for posterior sampling’s effectiveness and can provably fail on sparse-reward problems.

The analysis also finds that propagating uncertainty does not rule out these failures, despite its previously emphasized role in exploration. Using these insights, the authors develop Successor Uncertainties, an inexpensive and straightforward randomized-value-function algorithm that retains key properties of posterior sampling. The design therefore follows from examining what existing approximations fail to preserve.

Successor Uncertainties performs strongly on difficult tabular exploration benchmarks. On Atari, it exceeds human performance on 38 of 49 tested games and achieves a median human-normalized score of 2.09. It also beats Bootstrapped DQN on 36 tested games. These results support the algorithm’s exploration strategy across both the tabular benchmarks and the evaluated game domain.
neurips-2019-successor-uncertainties-exp.tldr: Successor Uncertainties preserves key posterior-sampling properties to address exploration failures in randomized value-function methods.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems require parameters to remain on a manifold, a constrained geometric space. This paper studies how to turn such problems into unconstrained ones by expressing their parameters through ordinary Euclidean coordinates. It calls these parameterizations trivializations and develops conditions under which they are sound for gradient-based optimization.

The authors examine two broad families of trivializations that have favorable properties but also share a performance problem. They introduce dynamic trivializations to resolve that issue. These methods sit between fixed parameterization-based optimization and Riemannian gradient descent, with the aim of combining benefits from both ways of handling the geometry.

The work also explains practical implementations for different matrix manifolds and proves a formula for the gradient of the matrix exponential. That formula is an additional computational contribution supporting the framework. On standard neural-network tasks designed to evaluate long-term memory, dynamic trivializations improve existing methods, providing empirical evidence that the geometric optimization approach can help in these learning settings.
neurips-2019-trivializations-for-gradien.tldr: Dynamic trivializations improve manifold-constrained optimization by combining parameterization-based methods with aspects of Riemannian gradient descent.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent can spend extra computation learning from stored experiences or from a learned environment model. This paper compares these options and emphasizes that experience replay also supports planning: it can improve predictions and behavior without collecting additional data. The question becomes what a parametric model adds beyond that capability.

The authors hypothesize that replay can match or outperform model-based learning under suitable conditions when the model only generates fictional transitions from observed states for an otherwise model-free update. Atari experiments support this hypothesis. The replay-based method achieves state-of-the-art data efficiency and improves on prior results using parametric models in the comparison described.

The paper also examines other uses of models. For credit assignment, backward planning can work better than forward planning. For choosing immediate behavior, forward planning can be beneficial. These findings make the model’s role central to the comparison: the value of learning an environment model depends partly on how its predictions are used to support learning or action selection.
neurips-2019-when-to-use-parametric-mode.tldr: The benefits of learned reinforcement-learning models depend on their use, with replay competitive under suitable conditions and planning direction affecting results.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning aims to recognize classes that have no training examples, typically using semantic descriptions to connect them with observed classes. This paper proposes giving a model generated experience of unseen classes as well. The goal is to learn about both seen and unseen classes within one generative modeling process.

The method uses a variational autoencoder with a class-specific multimodal prior to learn class-conditional distributions. It treats absent examples of unseen classes as missing data. Training then alternates between generating those examples and learning model parameters, jointly seeking useful unseen datapoints and a model that accounts for both groups of classes.

Because the resulting model provides conditional generation for seen and unseen classes, it can perform classification and generation directly without an additional off-the-shelf classifier. Experiments report better performance than training only on seen classes and than several state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the proposed iterative interaction between generating missing examples and learning from them as a way to address the lack of observed unseen-class data.
neurips-2019-zero-shot-learning-via-simu.tldr: A generative zero-shot model alternates between creating unseen-class examples and learning to classify and generate across seen and unseen classes.
